summary: Choose Server or Client Components, control freshness and caching, build Route Handlers, and protect the edge with middleware.

lessons.title: Server Components and the client boundary
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of the server/client separation in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of the server/client separation.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: Components are server by default: they can await the database, read secrets, and send only serialized results. The use client directive creates a transitive boundary for interaction; props crossing it must be serializable. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: the server/client separation is like a restaurant where the kitchen keeps secrets and data, the dining room handles interaction, and the pass checks every order. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

A Server Component moves fetching close to the source, avoids a browser/API round trip, and keeps a service-role client out of the public bundle. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

A Client Component can receive name, price, and identifier, but not an arbitrary server function, DB connection, or non-serializable object. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

Putting use client high in the tree needlessly turns imports into client bundle code; moving the boundary down to the button reduces JavaScript and attack surface. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

lessons.title: Cache, freshness, and revalidation
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of a data freshness policy in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of a data freshness policy.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: Caching is a temporal contract: it trades freshness for less work and faster responses. Data needs a policy based on volatility and domain risk, not one setting for the entire application. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: a data freshness policy is like a restaurant where the kitchen keeps secrets and data, the dining room handles interaction, and the pass checks every order. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

A public catalog may accept five minutes of caching, while checkout stock, session, and permissions must be read at the critical moment. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

revalidate: 300 allows a new version after the window; a tag groups reads that a product mutation should deliberately invalidate. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

no-store forces a fresh read but increases latency and load; it fits personalized or critical data, not every request by default. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

lessons.title: Route Handlers and HTTP contracts
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of design of an HTTP route in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of design of an HTTP route.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: route.ts exposes a network boundary with one function per HTTP method. It reads Request, authenticates and validates before any write, calls domain logic, and translates the result into stable status, headers, and JSON. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: design of an HTTP route is like a restaurant where the kitchen keeps secrets and data, the dining room handles interaction, and the pass checks every order. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

GET reads query and does not mutate state; POST creates, PATCH partially updates, and DELETE removes under a documented and idempotent contract when required. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

lessons.title: Middleware, cookies, and redirects
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of early request filtering in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of early request filtering.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: Middleware runs before routes matching its matcher and can continue, redirect, or enrich a response. It improves navigation and broad protection, but the sensitive route must still verify session and permission when acting. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: early request filtering is like a restaurant where the kitchen keeps secrets and data, the dining room handles interaction, and the pass checks every order. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

A narrow matcher avoids running middleware on images, scripts, and public pages; each edge millisecond repeats across many requests. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

Cookie presence is not proof of authenticity: a session must be signed, unexpired, and verified again before data access. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

The next parameter improves post-login return but must be restricted to an internal path to prevent an open redirect to a malicious site. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.
